transcript.content: Hello, welcome. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

I guess… I’m here because I haven’t been myself since my daughter left for basic training. It sounds dramatic when I say it out loud, but the house just feels dead when I come home now. Like all the noise got sucked out of it, and I walk in after work and I don’t know what to do with myself.

I’ve been crying in my truck before shifts, which is not like me. I’m a sheet metal worker, I weld, I’ve been doing this stuff for years, and lately I’m missing steps on jobs I could practically do in my sleep. Then I get mad at myself, and I end up snapping at the younger guys at work when they’re not even doing anything that bad.

And I used to go out on the water, or mess around with my sculpture, you know, things that made me feel like I had a life outside the shop. But I just… don’t. I don’t see the point right now. I keep thinking I should be handling this better, she’s doing something good, but I can’t seem to keep myself together.
Have you had similar episodes like this before, or is this the first time you’ve felt this way since your daughter left?

No, not like this. I mean, I’ve had bad stretches before, sure—everybody does, work stress, bills, family stuff—but I was managing okay before she shipped out. I was functioning, going to work, coming home, doing my normal routine.

This really started after she left for basic training. Not the exact same day, maybe, because at first I think I was running on adrenaline and trying to be proud and busy, but within a few weeks it just kind of hit me. The quiet in the house, not having her around, not knowing what to do with all that space… that’s when I started feeling like I couldn’t get my feet under me. So, no, I wouldn’t say I’ve had an episode like this before. It feels tied to her leaving.

How often have you been feeling this way—like you can’t get your feet under you, not enjoying things, and feeling down—have these feelings been happening most days, or do they come and go more randomly?

It’s most days. I wish I could say it just hits me here and there, like a bad hour and then I shake it off, but it’s been pretty constant since she left.

Especially when I come home. That’s when it really settles on me—the house feels dead, like there’s no life in it. I’ll make it through work barely holding it together, and then I get home and it’s just… quiet. Too quiet. And then the next morning I’m sitting in my truck before my shift crying, trying to pull myself together before anybody sees me.

And it’s not just feeling sad, either. It’s like I can’t get steady. I’m missing steps on welding jobs I’ve done for years, stuff I should know without even thinking. Then I get frustrated and I snap at the younger guys, and afterward I feel awful because they didn’t really deserve it. I used to go out on the water or work on my sculpture to clear my head, but lately I just don’t see the point, so I don’t do it.

So yeah… it’s pretty much most days. Some moments are worse than others, but it’s there a lot.
Have you noticed that you feel more tired than usual, or that you don’t have the energy to do things you normally would?

I’m not really sure how to answer that. I mean… I feel worn down, but I don’t know if it’s tired like sleep-tired, or just… emotionally wrung out, if that makes sense.

I haven’t been paying close attention to my energy in that way. Some days I get through what I have to do because I have to, and then I come home and just kind of stop. But I don’t know that I’d say I’ve noticed a clear change like, “Oh, I’m exhausted all the time.” It’s more that everything feels heavier than it used to, but I’m not sure if that’s the same thing you’re asking.
Have you noticed that things you used to enjoy, like going out on the water or working on your sculpture, don’t feel as rewarding or pleasurable as they used to?

Yeah… yes. That’s actually one of the parts that scares me, because those were the things that used to make me feel like myself.

Going out on the water was kind of my reset button, you know? Even if work was rough or I was annoyed about something, I could get out there and breathe, and it would settle me down. And my sculpture—I used to lose hours with that. I’d start messing with a piece and forget everything else for a while.

But since my daughter left for basic training, it’s like I come home and the house just feels dead. Quiet in a way that gets under my skin. And I’ll think, “Maybe I should go out,” or “Maybe I should work on something,” but then it’s like… what’s the point? It doesn’t pull me the way it used to. I don’t get that feeling from it.

I’ve mostly just stopped doing those things. I keep telling myself I should, because I know they used to help, but they don’t feel rewarding right now. It’s like everything that used to have life in it went flat after she left.
Has this loss of interest or pleasure in things you used to enjoy, like going out on the water or working on your sculpture, been happening every day or nearly every day for most of the day?

Yeah… I mean, pretty close to that. I don’t know if I can say literally every minute of every day, because at work I can sometimes get pulled into a task for a bit, but even then it’s like I’m just going through the motions.

Since my daughter left for basic training, it’s been most days, and a lot of the day. I come home and the house feels dead, and that’s when it really hits me. I used to think, “I’ll get out on the water,” or “I’ll go work on the sculpture,” but now I just kind of look at it and think… what’s the point? It doesn’t give me that feeling anymore.

And it’s not like I’m choosing to be lazy or anything. I want to want those things, if that makes sense. I want them to help the way they used to. But most days I’m just trying to keep myself together—crying in my truck before shifts, messing up welding steps I’ve done a hundred times, snapping at the younger guys—and by the time I’m home, I don’t have that pull toward anything. It all just feels flat.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight since your daughter left for basic training?

I don’t really know. I haven’t been tracking it, honestly.

I mean, I’m eating, but I couldn’t tell you if it’s more or less than before in any clear way. Some days I realize I just grabbed whatever was easy, but I don’t know if that’s an appetite thing or just me not wanting to make a whole meal for myself. And I haven’t weighed myself or noticed my clothes fitting different or anything like that.

So… no, not that I’ve clearly noticed. It’s not something that’s stood out to me the way the other stuff has.
Have you been feeling like you’re not good enough or blaming yourself for things more than usual since your daughter left?

I don’t know… not in a clear way, I guess.

I mean, I’ve had thoughts like, “Maybe I should be handling this better,” or “Other parents probably don’t fall apart like this,” but I don’t know if that’s the same as feeling like I’m not good enough. It’s more like I’m frustrated with myself for not being able to just adjust and be normal about it.

But I wouldn’t say I’m walking around thinking everything is my fault, or that I failed her or anything like that. She left to do something she chose, and I know that. I’m proud of her. It’s just… I don’t know. I get upset with myself for being so affected by it, but I haven’t really noticed some big change where I’m blaming myself for things more than usual.
Have you noticed that you’ve been moving more slowly than usual, or that you can’t sit still and feel restless?

I’m not really sure. I haven’t noticed myself moving slower in the way you mean, like physically dragging my feet or people telling me I’m slowed down or anything like that.

And I don’t think I’ve been restless like pacing around the house nonstop or unable to sit in a chair. I mean, sometimes I don’t feel settled, but I don’t know if that’s the same thing. I haven’t really been paying attention to my movements, honestly. The things I’ve noticed have been more… just how hard it is to get myself to do things, not that my body is obviously slower or wired up.

So I guess my answer is: not that I’ve clearly noticed.
Have you ever felt so overwhelmed or down that you’ve thought about hurting yourself or that life wasn’t worth living?

I… I don’t really know how to answer that exactly.

I’ve definitely felt overwhelmed, like really overwhelmed, but as far as hurting myself or thinking life isn’t worth living… I don’t think I’ve had it in that clear kind of way. Not like making a plan or wanting to do something to myself.

Sometimes I’ve had moments where I just think, “I can’t keep feeling like this,” or I wish I could shut my brain off for a while, but I don’t know if that’s what you mean. It’s more like wanting a break from feeling so wound up and upset, not wanting to die. I don’t want to hurt myself.

So… no, I guess not in the way you’re asking. It’s been hard, but I haven’t been thinking about ending my life or anything like that.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep since your daughter left for basic training, like trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or sleeping more than usual?

I’m honestly not totally sure how to answer that, because I haven’t really been keeping track of it in a clear way.

Since she left, I know my nights feel different, but I don’t know if I’d say, “Yes, I have insomnia,” or anything like that. Some nights I lie there thinking about her and wondering what she’s doing, whether she’s okay, whether she’s having a hard time, and then I realize more time has passed than I thought. But I don’t know if that counts as trouble falling asleep, or if it’s just… being a mom and having too much in my head.

I don’t think I’m sleeping more than usual. If anything, I just feel like sleep hasn’t been very satisfying, but I’m not sure if I’m waking up a lot or if I’m just aware of feeling unsettled when I go to bed. I’m sorry, I know that’s not a very exact answer. I guess I’ve noticed that bedtime is harder emotionally, but I haven’t really measured whether my actual sleep is much different.
Would you say that your mood has been down most of the day, nearly every day, since your daughter left for basic training?

Yeah… I think so. I mean, I don’t know if I’d say every single minute of every day, but since my daughter left for basic training, it’s like something in the house just went quiet in a bad way.

I come home and it feels like a dead house. I know that sounds dramatic, but that’s what it feels like. I’ll walk in after work and there’s no noise, no sign of her stuff, no reason to ask how her day was, and I just… I fall apart more than I want to admit. I keep thinking I should be proud and strong and all that, and I am proud of her, I really am, but it doesn’t stop this heavy feeling.

It’s been most days, yeah. I’ve cried in my truck before going in for shifts, trying to get myself together before anyone sees me. And at work I’m not myself. I’ve missed steps on welding jobs I’ve done for years, stuff I shouldn’t even have to think about, and then I get mad at myself and snap at the younger guys when they don’t deserve it.

And when I’m not working, I’m not doing the things that usually make me feel like me. I haven’t been going out on the water, and I haven’t been working on my sculpture. I just look at it and think, what’s the point? So… yeah, I guess my mood has been down a lot of the day, nearly every day. It’s not just missing her for a few minutes here and there. It’s kind of sitting on everything.
Have you noticed that it's been harder to think clearly, concentrate, or make decisions since your daughter left for basic training?

Yeah… yes. I think that’s actually one of the things that scares me the most, because it’s not like me.

At work, I do welding jobs I’ve done for years. I mean, years. Things my hands usually know before my brain even catches up, if that makes sense. And lately I’ll be in the middle of something and realize I missed a step, or I’ll have to stop and stare at it like, “What was I just doing?” Then I get embarrassed and angry at myself, and I end up snapping at the younger guys when they ask something or get in my way, and they don’t deserve that. It’s like I’m there, but I’m not fully there.

And before shifts, I’ve been sitting in my truck trying to pull myself together, crying, wiping my face, telling myself, “You have to go in there and act normal.” So by the time I actually get inside, I’m already worn out. My head feels crowded, like part of me is trying to do the job and part of me is still thinking about my daughter being gone and coming home later to that dead, empty house.

Even outside work, decisions feel harder. I don’t even really decide not to go out on the water or not to work on my sculpture—I just… don’t. I look at those things and I can’t get myself to start. It all feels like too much effort, or like I don’t see the point right now. So, yeah, I’d say thinking clearly and concentrating have definitely been harder since she left.

inference_history.note: The patient is presenting with symptoms of depressed mood, anhedonia, emotional lability, and difficulty concentrating following a psychosocial stressor (daughter leaving for basic training). This suggests a possible diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder (F32.9) or Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood (F43.22). Differentiation will depend on further assessment of symptom duration, severity, and impairment in functioning.

It’s been most days, yeah. I’ve cried in my truck before going in for shifts, trying to get myself together before anyone sees me. And at work I’m not myself. I’ve missed steps on welding jobs I’ve done for years, stuff I shouldn’t even have to think about, and then I get mad at myself and snap at the younger guys when they don’t deserve it.

And when I’m not working, I’m not doing the things that usually make me feel like me. I haven’t been going out on the water, and I haven’t been working on my sculpture. I just look at it and think, what’s the point? So… yeah, I guess my mood has been down a lot of the day, nearly every day. It’s not just missing her for a few minutes here and there. It’s kind of sitting on everything.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced a diminished ability to think or concentrate, which is relevant for differentiating between F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder, single episode, unspecified) and F43.22 (Adjustment Disorder with Depressed Mood).
doctor.question: Have you noticed that it's been harder to think clearly, concentrate, or make decisions since your daughter left for basic training?

target_item.name: Stress_Related_Maladaptive_Response
target_item.manifestation: Since my daughter left for basic training, I feel like I come home to a dead house and I can’t keep myself together—I'm crying in the truck before shifts, missing steps on welding jobs I’ve done for years, snapping at the younger guys, and I’ve stopped going out on the water or working on my sculpture because I just don’t see the point.
target_item.reason: The question asks about trouble thinking clearly, concentrating, or making decisions since the identifiable stressor of the daughter leaving, which is reflected in missing steps on familiar welding jobs as part of the stress-related maladaptive response.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yes. I think that’s actually one of the things that scares me the most, because it’s not like me.

At work, I do welding jobs I’ve done for years. I mean, years. Things my hands usually know before my brain even catches up, if that makes sense. And lately I’ll be in the middle of something and realize I missed a step, or I’ll have to stop and stare at it like, “What was I just doing?” Then I get embarrassed and angry at myself, and I end up snapping at the younger guys when they ask something or get in my way, and they don’t deserve that. It’s like I’m there, but I’m not fully there.

And before shifts, I’ve been sitting in my truck trying to pull myself together, crying, wiping my face, telling myself, “You have to go in there and act normal.” So by the time I actually get inside, I’m already worn out. My head feels crowded, like part of me is trying to do the job and part of me is still thinking about my daughter being gone and coming home later to that dead, empty house.

Even outside work, decisions feel harder. I don’t even really decide not to go out on the water or not to work on my sculpture—I just… don’t. I look at those things and I can’t get myself to start. It all feels like too much effort, or like I don’t see the point right now. So, yeah, I’d say thinking clearly and concentrating have definitely been harder since she left.

There is no evidence of a major depressive episode meeting full criteria, as symptoms have not been persistent enough across all domains (e.g., no clear changes in sleep, appetite, or self-esteem) to warrant a diagnosis of major depressive disorder.
